ddx.step1_summary:
- Chief complaint: 3 days of profuse watery diarrhoea
- Symptoms: watery stools nearly every hour while awake; crampy lower/central abdominal pain, intermittent, pain severity ~6/10 when present; nausea with at least one vomiting episode after milk; subjective fever/hot sensations (no measured temperature); decreased urinary frequency; feels fluids pass rapidly through (poor stool form); onset ~3 days ago; not improving.
- Past medical history: Patient reports otherwise fit and well; no chronic medical conditions recalled.
- Medications / Allergies: No regular medications. Taking paracetamol PRN. No known drug allergies.
- Family / Social history: Father with stage 3 colon cancer. Brother recently had a similar diarrhoeal illness for ~5 days and is improving. Lives with mother and sister. Works in an office. Social smoker and occasional/heavy alcohol use 1–2 times/month.
- Vital signs / exam findings: No objective vitals recorded. No physical exam documented (telephone/telehealth visit). Patient reports feeling hot and less frequent urine (possible dehydration).
- Labs / imaging: None mentioned or performed.

V: Mesenteric ischemia: Unlikely but can present with severe abdominal pain and diarrhoea; less likely in a young, otherwise healthy 27-year-old with intermittent cramping and high stool frequency and no risk factors.
I: Viral gastroenteritis (e.g., norovirus, rotavirus): Common cause of acute watery diarrhoea with nausea, vomiting, crampy abdominal pain, short 1–3 day course — consistent with rapid onset, high stool frequency, and similar illness in a household contact (brother).

Bacterial foodborne gastroenteritis (e.g., enterotoxigenic E. coli, Salmonella, Campylobacter): Can cause profuse watery diarrhoea, cramping and fever; possible if exposed to contaminated food or shared exposure with brother.

Foodborne toxin (Staphylococcal/Bacillus cereus): Causes rapid-onset vomiting and/or diarrhoea after contaminated food — vomiting after milk could reflect ingested trigger, though predominant diarrhoea favors other enteric infections.
N: Colorectal neoplasm: Family history of colon cancer is relevant for long-term risk, but new acute profuse watery diarrhoea in a 27-year-old is unlikely due to malignancy.
D: Secondary lactose intolerance (post-infectious): Acute gastroenteritis can transiently cause lactase deficiency leading to bloating, cramping and vomiting after milk — fits vomiting with milk and loose stools.
Chronic malabsorption (less likely acute): e.g., celiac disease typically produces chronic symptoms rather than an acute 3-day illness.
I2: Medication-induced diarrhoea (e.g., antibiotics, laxatives): Patient reports no regular medications or recent antibiotics, so iatrogenic cause is unlikely.
Alcohol/toxin ingestion: Heavy episodic alcohol or ingested toxin could cause GI upset, but course and household contact make infectious cause more likely.
C: Congenital GI conditions (e.g., congenital bile salt malabsorption): Unlikely to present acutely in adulthood with this pattern; not suggested by history.
A: Food allergy (e.g., IgE-mediated to milk): IgE food allergy typically causes immediate vomiting, urticaria or anaphylaxis; isolated delayed watery diarrhoea without other allergic signs is less consistent.
T: Traumatic/obstructive causes: No history of abdominal trauma or signs of obstruction; presentation favors diarrhoeal illness rather than trauma.
E: Hyperthyroidism: Can cause chronic diarrhoea and heat intolerance, but acute 3-day profuse watery diarrhoea with vomiting and household case favors infectious gastroenteritis.
Electrolyte disturbance / dehydration: Consequence of high stool output rather than primary cause — relevant as a complication (reduced urine frequency, feeling hot).

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Acute onset (3 days) of frequent watery diarrhoea, crampy abdominal pain, nausea/vomiting, subjective fever, and a household contact (brother) with a similar self-limited illness strongly supports a viral gastroenteritis.
supporting_evidence: 3-day history of profuse watery diarrhoea occurring hourly
Nausea and at least one vomiting episode
Brother had similar diarrhoeal illness (household/close-contact spread)
No chronic GI history, rapid onset and likely self-limited course
opposing_evidence: No documented fever measurement or exam/vitals to confirm systemic signs
Vomiting after milk raises consideration of lactose intolerance or food-specific reaction, though this can co-occur

step3_ranked_ddx.diagnosis: Bacterial foodborne gastroenteritis (e.g., enterotoxigenic E. coli, Salmonella, Campylobacter)
step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Bacterial pathogens can present with profuse diarrhoea, cramping and subjective fever. A shared exposure with brother or contaminated food could explain simultaneous illness; some bacterial causes produce more severe or prolonged symptoms.
supporting_evidence: Profuse watery diarrhoea with cramping and subjective fever
Possible shared exposure given brother's similar illness
Vomiting (may be present in some bacterial etiologies)
opposing_evidence: No bloody stools reported (some bacterial infections cause bloody diarrhoea)
Rapid improvement typical for viral illness and no severe systemic features documented (e.g., high fever, severe dehydration, sepsis)
No history of recent antibiotic use or specific food exposure recalled

step3_ranked_ddx.diagnosis: Secondary lactose intolerance (transient post-infectious lactase deficiency) or primary lactose intolerance unmasked
step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Patient vomited after drinking milk and reports feeling worse with milk; following an enteric infection patients can develop transient lactase deficiency producing loose stools, cramping and nausea particularly after dairy intake.
supporting_evidence: Crampy abdominal pain and watery stools which can worsen with lactose ingestion
Acute gastroenteritis is already suspected which can precipitate secondary lactose intolerance
opposing_evidence: Primary lactose intolerance usually causes bloating, flatulence and diarrhea after dairy rather than hourly profuse watery diarrhoea; patient reports high stool frequency throughout day which suggests a broader infectious process
Brother's similar illness suggests transmissible agent rather than isolated lactose intolerance

step3_ranked_ddx.diagnosis: Inflammatory bowel disease (Crohn's disease or ulcerative colitis)
step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: IBD can present with abdominal pain and diarrhoea, but typically causes a more subacute-to-chronic course with blood/mucus, weight loss and extraintestinal features; acute onset over 3 days with household contact and profuse watery stools favors infection.
supporting_evidence: Crampy abdominal pain and diarrhoea are compatible with IBD symptoms in general
Family history of colon cancer (relevant for surveillance but not diagnostic)
opposing_evidence: Acute 3-day course with a household contact is more consistent with infectious gastroenteritis
No blood or mucus reported in stool, no chronic pattern, no prior history of similar flares

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Ingestion of preformed toxins (e.g., Staphylococcus aureus) can cause vomiting and diarrhoea; however the presence of a household contact and predominant watery diarrhoea over several days make viral or bacterial infection more likely than a short-lived toxin-mediated illness.
supporting_evidence: Acute GI symptoms including vomiting and diarrhoea could be due to contaminated food
opposing_evidence: No specific recent shared meal or food source identified
Toxin-mediated food poisoning often causes very rapid onset (hours) and profuse vomiting which is not the dominant feature here
